text.en: On a clear night Raju saw a milky band across the sky. "That is our galaxy, the Milky Way," said his grandfather.

Observations indicate that the universe has expanded from a hot, dense early state for about thirteen point eight billion years. This description is known as the Big Bang model. The part we can observe is called the observable universe. Stars are grouped in galaxies, and our galaxy is the Milky Way, so named because it appears as a milky band of light. On a sky map, familiar star patterns help us identify constellations. Astronomers also use constellation names for defined regions of the sky.
The solar system has the Sun at the centre, which is a star, with eight planets going round it along paths called orbits. The time for one revolution is the period of revolution and the time for one rotation is the period of rotation. The four inner planets are rocky. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, and Uranus and Neptune are known as ice giants.
The solar system includes natural satellites, asteroids, comets and small bodies called meteoroids. A meteor is a streak of light made when a meteoroid enters an atmosphere. Kepler's laws describe how planets move around the Sun, and an object orbiting the Earth needs a certain orbital velocity. The International Space Station is a laboratory in orbit built by many nations working together.

Begin with Earth orbiting the Sun. The solar system belongs to the Milky Way, which is one galaxy in the universe. These names describe structures on different scales.

board.text: Earth → Solar System → Milky Way → universe

text.en: Light takes time to cross space. When a distant star sends light toward us, we receive a record of the star as it was when the light left it.

board.text: Looking farther can also mean looking into the past

text.en: A light-year is a distance. It is how far light travels in a vacuum in one year. A star ten light-years away sends light that takes about ten years to reach us.
The observable universe is limited by which signals have had time to reach us. This limit describes what we can see from our location. It gives no direct view beyond that limit.

board.text: Observable range depends on arriving signals

text.en: Distant galaxies can show light shifted toward longer wavelengths. The pattern of shifts across many galaxies is one line of evidence that the universe is expanding.
A galaxy is a large collection of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. On a dark night, part of the Milky Way can look like a hazy band because we look along its crowded disk.
Two stars may appear close together on a sky chart while actually lying at different distances from Earth. A constellation pattern is what we see from our viewpoint.

board.text: A sky pattern records apparent directions

text.en: The Sun gives off its own light. Planets look bright partly because their surfaces or atmospheres reflect sunlight toward us.

board.text: Stars give off light; planets can reflect it

text.en: Moving away from the Sun, name the four rocky planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Then name Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

board.text: Order from Sun: Mercury to Neptune

text.en: An asteroid is often rocky or metallic. A comet often contains ice and dust and can grow a tail as it gets closer to the Sun.

board.text: Asteroid and comet are types of small body

text.en: A piece travelling through space can be called a meteoroid. Its streak of light in the atmosphere is a meteor. If a fragment survives to reach the ground, it is a meteorite.

board.text: Meteoroid → meteor → meteorite if a piece lands

text.en: Rotation is spinning around an axis. Revolution is travelling around another body. Earth turns on its axis while also completing an orbit around the Sun.
Kepler’s first law describes a planet’s orbit as an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. A circle is a special case of an ellipse, and many real planet orbits are close to circular.

board.text: Elliptical orbit · Sun at one focus

text.en: Kepler’s second law compares the areas swept as a line joins the Sun and the planet. Equal time intervals sweep equal areas. Near the Sun, the planet travels farther along its path in the same time.
Kepler’s third law compares planets sharing the same central body. The square of orbital period is proportional to the cube of the orbit’s semi-major axis.
In a model with one orbit four times the size of another by semi-major axis, the period squared is sixty-four times greater. The period itself is eight times greater.
The Moon is a natural satellite of Earth. An artificial satellite is placed in orbit by people. Some artificial satellites collect weather observations or relay signals.
A satellite has a sideways velocity while gravity pulls it toward Earth. The inward acceleration keeps curving its path. The satellite can keep missing the surface while it falls under gravity.
For circular orbits around Earth in a simple model, a satellite farther from Earth’s centre moves more slowly and takes longer to finish one orbit.

board.text: Larger circular orbit → slower speed, longer period

text.en: The International Space Station is a laboratory orbiting Earth. People and loose objects float inside because the station and its contents are falling together around Earth.

board.text: ISS: orbiting laboratory · shared free fall

text.en: International teams share tools and observations on the station. Work there can compare how materials or instruments behave under conditions that are difficult to reproduce on the ground.
When you describe a path, identify the body being orbited and the orbit’s shape. When you describe a time, identify whether it is the time for a spin or a full orbit.

board.text: Ask which body, which path and which period

problem.en: Two planets orbit the same star. If the second orbit has four times the semi-major axis, how do the orbital periods compare?

text.en: Cube the semi-major-axis ratio of four.

why.en: Kepler’s third law gives sixty-four as the ratio of the period squares.

text.en: Take the positive square root of sixty-four.

why.en: The second period is eight times the first.

prompt.en: A friend says The Earth is at the centre of the universe. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Early people thought so before telescopes.
The Earth is one planet going round the Sun, in one galaxy among many.

points.en: The universe has expanded from a hot, dense early state for about 13.8 billion years.
The Milky Way is our galaxy.
The inner planets are rocky. The outer planets include two gas giants and two ice giants.
The ISS is an international laboratory in space.
